title: Bahrain | CBB Cyber Security Risk Management (Module OM) and Confidentiality
tagline: The CBB's Module OM-5.5 cyber rules in practice: governance, phishing defences, one-hour incident reporting, confidentiality and staff training.
sectors: Conventional banks licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain
IT, cyber security and security operations
Contact centres, branches and digital channels
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **conventional banks licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB)**. It is built on **Section OM-5.5 (Cyber Security Risk Management) of the Operational Risk Management Module in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook**, the **confidentiality articles (116-119) of the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law (Law No. 64 of 2006)**, and, in general terms only, the **Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018)**.

Module OM content comes from the **CBB-hosted copy of Volume 1, Module OM issued with the CBB's consultation of 28 January 2024**. Pages dated 2021-2022 show the rules then in force; pages marked 'XX 2024' are treated as proposals. The consolidated Rulebook site could not be opened, so always check the current paragraph. Volume 1 only; other volumes are not covered.

OM-5.5.55 requires all employees to receive regular cyber security training, and OM-5.5.56 adds role-specific training for the board, senior management, cyber, IT and high-risk staff. This quest covers governance, prevention and phishing, testing, incident reporting to the CBB, confidentiality and training effectiveness.

This quest builds knowledge of the Bahrain framework; it does not replace your institution's own cyber security, information security and data protection policies, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees of CBB-licensed conventional banks who need the cyber awareness training Module OM requires
Contact centre, branch, payments and digital banking staff exposed to phishing and social engineering
IT, cyber security and SOC staff who apply the OM-5.5 controls and incident reporting rules
Board members and senior managers who oversee cyber risk and receive role-specific training
Risk, compliance, data protection and internal audit staff preparing for CBB reviews
outcomes: Explain the board, senior management, CISO and cyber risk function duties under Module OM-5.5
Apply the preventive, email authentication and customer-link controls in OM-5.5.18 to OM-5.5.21
Recognise phishing and social engineering and respond with pause, verify and report
Describe the testing cycles and apply the one-hour, two-hour and 10-day CBB incident reporting steps
Apply the confidentiality gateways in Articles 116-117 of the CBB Law and describe the PDPL in general terms
Design and measure role-based cyber training that meets OM-5.5.54 to OM-5.5.56

quest.name: Shields of the Kingdom
quest.premise: You have just joined the cyber risk team at Dilmun Coast Bank, a fictional conventional retail bank licensed by the CBB, with its head office in Seef, Manama, and branches in Riffa and Muharraq. Phishing texts are hitting customers and the board wants proof the bank's cyber programme works. With CISO Fatema Al Sayed, SOC lead Arjun Pillai, contact centre supervisor Maryam Al Mahroos and CRO Thomas Brennan, clear five stages, then face the final boss: chief executive Rashid Bucheeri's board review.

sessions.title: Bahrain's Cyber Rulebook: Module OM-5.5 and Who Owns Cyber Risk
sessions.summary: Map the CBB's cyber security rules for conventional banks in Module OM-5.5: the board's role, the NIST-based framework, the independent cyber risk function and CISO, senior management duties and review cycles, and which version of the text this quest uses.
objectives: Explain how Module OM-5.5 in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook applies to conventional banks and which CBB-hosted version this quest uses
Describe the duties of the board, the cyber security committee, senior management and the CISO
List the minimum components of the cyber framework and its review cycles
Explain why the cyber risk function must be independent of IT

cards.title: Day one in the CISO's office
cards.setting: Dilmun Coast Bank head office, Seef, Manama. 8:15 am.

lines.text: You join Dilmun Coast Bank, a fictional conventional retail bank licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain, on the cyber risk team.
Welcome! I'm Fatema Al Sayed, the bank's CISO. Your quest starts with a question the CBB will ask us: who owns cyber risk here?
Arjun Pillai, SOC team lead. Most people say 'IT'. That's the wrong answer in Bahrain.
Module OM, Section OM-5.5, puts the board at the top, senior management in charge of delivery and a cyber risk function that sits outside IT.
Thomas Brennan, Chief Risk Officer. I chair our cyber security committee, so that function reports into my side of the house.
And I'm Rashid Bucheeri, chief executive. Cyber is on every board agenda now. I want to know we can show the CBB a working framework, not just a policy file.
Then let's map it. By the end of this stage you'll know the framework, the roles and the review cycles.

scenes.heading: The board owns it
scenes.narration: The board must make sure the bank has a robust cyber security risk management policy, approve it and set clear ownership and accountability. Cyber security must be discussed at board or board committee meetings.

scenes.heading: A framework built on NIST
scenes.narration: The framework must contain a cyber strategy, a cyber policy, a risk approach with tools and methods, and an organisation-wide security awareness programme. It follows the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.

scenes.heading: Independent of IT
scenes.narration: A cyber security risk function, separate from the IT department, reports to an independent risk function and monitors how mature the controls are. A suitably qualified CISO heads it.

scenes.heading: Senior management delivers
scenes.narration: Senior management builds and runs the framework, writes the strategy and policy, allocates resources and reports to the board at least quarterly on threats and incidents.

scenes.heading: Reviewed on a cycle
scenes.narration: The board re-evaluates the framework every three years or sooner when risks change. The strategy is revised at least every three years, and the policy is reviewed and approved at least once a year.

cards.title: Who owns cyber risk at a Bahraini conventional bank
cards.caption: Based on OM-5.5.1 to OM-5.5.11 in the CBB-hosted Module OM copy issued with the January 2024 consultation.

items.label: Board of directors
items.detail: Approves the cyber policy and framework, sets accountability, discusses cyber at meetings.

items.label: Cyber security committee
items.detail: Headed by an independent control-function senior manager such as the CRO or CFO.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Builds and runs the framework, resources it and reports to the board at least quarterly.

items.label: Cyber risk function and CISO
items.detail: Independent of IT; monitors and reports on control status and maturity.

items.label: Every employee
items.detail: Follows the policy, completes training and reports suspicious activity.

cards.title: Match the duty to its owner
cards.prompt: Link each OM-5.5 duty to the person or body that carries it.

pairs.right: Approves the cyber policy and re-evaluates the framework at least every three years
Reports to the board on cyber threats and risk treatment at least quarterly
Heads the cyber security risk function with authority to implement the strategy
Approves the policies and frameworks needed to carry out the cyber strategy
Monitors and reports on the status and maturity of cyber controls

cards.question: Under OM-5.5.6, where should Dilmun Coast Bank's cyber security risk function report?
options: To the head of IT, who runs the systems
To an independent risk management function or an equivalent
To the internal auditor only
Directly to the CBB
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.6 requires the cyber risk function to be independent of the IT department and to report to an independent risk management function or an equivalent. Reporting to IT would defeat that independence.

cards.title: Which text this quest uses
cards.body:
The consolidated CBB Rulebook site could not be opened for this quest, so its Module OM content comes from the **CBB-hosted copy of Volume 1, Module OM** published with the CBB's consultation of **28 January 2024** on proposed amendments to the cyber security requirements.

- Most of Section OM-5.5 in that copy carries pages dated **July 2021**, with some pages from **April 2022** and **October 2022**: these show the rules in force when the consultation was issued.
- Pages marked **'XX 2024'** show the **proposals**, such as making a cyber threat intelligence subscription mandatory and adding an external attack surface management platform. Treat these as proposals unless you confirm the final text.
- **Volume 1 covers conventional banks only.** Other volumes have their own versions of the rules.

Always check the current paragraph in the Rulebook and follow your bank's own policies.

cards.title: Rule or proposal?
cards.prompt: Sort each item from the January 2024 CBB copy of Module OM: was it already in the dated 2021-2022 pages, or a 2024 proposal?

items.text: Penetration testing at least twice a year
Calling the CBB within one hour of a qualifying cyber incident
Regular cyber training for all employees
A mandatory subscription to a cyber threat intelligence service
An external attack surface management platform
A CISO heading an independent cyber risk function
SPF, DKIM and DMARC email authentication

cards.title: The board pack
cards.setting: Board meeting preparation room, Seef. Two days before the board.

lines.text: The chairman wants one page on cyber. Can we just give him the number of incidents?
OM-5.5.4 expects fuller reports at every board meeting: key risk and performance indicators, control maturity, staff awareness status, recent incidents and penetration test results.
And senior management owes the board quarterly or more frequent reports on threats, risk treatment and all cyber incidents, internal and external.
Staff awareness is a board item too?
Yes. If the board can't see whether people are spotting phishing, it can't judge the risk.

cards.back: The documented, bank-wide plan: why cyber matters to the bank, its main threats, its approach, objectives and how it will respond, recover and share information. Revised at least every three years.
The written rules protecting systems and client data, covering roles, risk tolerance and functions such as access, incident and third-party management. Reviewed and approved at least annually.
A statement, in the policy, of how much cyber risk the bank accepts, shaped by customer impact, downtime, publicity, penalties and financial loss.
A regularly updated list of the bank's information assets and data, each with a clear internal owner and classification.
Deciding how important each set of data is and putting it in a category that sets who can access it, how it is protected, kept, encrypted and disposed of.
Approved plans and procedures for responding to and recovering from cyber incidents, with criteria for activating them.

cards.title: The IT director's proposal
cards.situation: To save costs, Dilmun Coast Bank's IT director proposes merging the cyber risk function into IT operations, with the CISO reporting to him. He argues that IT already runs the firewalls and knows the systems best. Rashid asks for your view before the executive committee.

choices.text: Support the merger, as IT has the technical expertise and one team is cheaper.
choices.outcome: The CBB expects the cyber risk function to be independent of IT and to report to an independent risk function. The merger would remove the challenge that independence is meant to give.

choices.text: Advise against it: OM-5.5.6 requires a cyber risk function independent of IT, reporting to risk, headed by a qualified CISO; propose better cooperation instead.
choices.outcome: Right. Independence lets the function monitor and report honestly on control maturity, including IT's own controls. Cooperation and shared tooling can save costs without changing the reporting line.

choices.text: Agree, but ask the IT director to send the CBB a quarterly letter confirming that controls are fine.
choices.outcome: Self-certification by the team being monitored is exactly what the rule avoids. The reporting line itself must stay independent.

choices.text: Suggest the CISO reports to IT for daily work and to the CRO once a year.
choices.outcome: This is partly right in spirit but still leaves the function inside IT for its day-to-day work. OM-5.5.6 asks for a function that is independent of IT.

cards.title: Real case: the CBB's January 2024 cyber consultation
cards.body:
On **28 January 2024** the CBB published proposed amendments to its cyber security requirements, with marked-up copies of Module OM for Volumes 1 and 2 and the matching modules for Volumes 5 and 6.

In the Volume 1 copy, the new pages (marked 'XX 2024') show the direction of travel:

- a cyber threat intelligence subscription moves from a recommendation to a **requirement**;
- banks would subscribe to an **external attack surface management** platform that continuously finds the bank's internet-facing assets, flags exposures with a data refresh within 24 to 48 hours, rates the bank's visible controls and profiles vendors and partners.

The lesson for Dilmun Coast Bank: Bahrain's cyber rules are updated in steps, through public consultation. Fatema keeps a watch list of consultations and checks the Rulebook before each annual policy review.

cards.question: How often must Dilmun Coast Bank's written cyber security policy be reviewed and approved under OM-5.5.15?
options: At least every three years
Only when the CBB asks
At least annually, by the board or senior management as appropriate
Every board meeting
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.15 requires the written cyber policy to be reviewed and approved at least annually by the board or senior management, as appropriate. The three-year cycle applies to the framework evaluation and the strategy revision.

cards.title: Read the verb
cards.body: The Rulebook marks binding rules with **must** and guidance with **should**. Both matter in an examination, but a 'must' gap is a breach. When the January 2024 copy changes a 'should' to a 'must', as for threat intelligence, the bank's plan has to change too. In policies, quote the paragraph number so reviewers can trace each control to OM-5.5.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: OM-5.5 in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook sets the cyber rules for conventional banks; this quest uses the CBB-hosted January 2024 consultation copy.
The board approves the cyber policy, sets accountability and discusses cyber at its meetings, with full cyber reports at every meeting.
The framework follows NIST and must include a strategy, a policy, a risk approach and an organisation-wide awareness programme.
A cyber risk function independent of IT, headed by a qualified CISO, reports to an independent risk function.
Cycles: framework evaluated every three years (or on major change), strategy revised at least every three years, policy approved at least annually.

cards.prompt: Who in your bank receives the board's cyber report, and does it include the status of staff security awareness? What would you add?

quiz.question: Which framework must a Bahraini conventional bank's cyber security risk management framework be developed in line with, according to OM-5.5.3?
options: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework
The PCI Data Security Standard
The Basel Committee's operational risk principles
ISO 22301 on business continuity
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.3 names the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, summarised in Appendix C of Module OM. The other standards may be useful but are not the one the rule names.

quiz.question: Which list matches the minimum components of the cyber framework in OM-5.5.2?
options: Strategy, policy, risk approach and tools, and an organisation-wide awareness programme
Strategy, insurance policy, penetration test results and a red team
Policy, firewall rules, antivirus software and a disaster recovery site
An IT budget, a vendor list, a help desk and an outsourcing contract
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.2 lists a cyber strategy, a cyber policy, a risk management approach with tools and methodology, and an organisation-wide security awareness programme. The other lists mix in controls or unrelated items.

quiz.question: Dilmun Coast Bank's board last evaluated its cyber framework 18 months ago. A major new threat emerges that changes the risk environment significantly. What does OM-5.5.5 expect?
options: Wait until the three-year point, as the cycle is fixed
A fresh board evaluation now, because significant change triggers it
Ask the CISO to update the framework without board involvement
Evaluate only at the next CBB inspection
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.5 requires the board to evaluate and approve the framework every three years or when there are significant changes to the risk environment. A major change brings the review forward.

quiz.question: Who should head the cyber security committee recommended by OM-5.5.9?
options: The head of IT infrastructure
An independent senior manager from a control function, such as the CFO or CRO
The external auditor
The most senior business line head
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.9 says the committee should be headed by an independent senior manager from a control function, giving examples such as the CFO or CRO. Its members should include business, IT, risk and compliance.

quiz.question: How often must senior management report to the board on cyber threats and cyber risk treatment under OM-5.5.10?
options: Once a year
Every three years
Only after a reportable incident
Quarterly or more often
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.10(e) requires quarterly or more frequent reports to the board on the current cyber threat situation and risk treatment, and (f) adds quarterly or more frequent reports on all cyber incidents.

quiz.question: Which item is listed in OM-5.5.4 as a topic for the comprehensive cyber reports the board should receive at every meeting?
options: The salary of the CISO
The status of staff information security awareness
The marketing plan for digital channels
Individual customers' account balances
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.4 lists key risk and performance indicators, control maturity status, staff information security awareness status, recent incidents and penetration test results.

quiz.question: A branch of a foreign bank operates in Bahrain under Volume 1. How does OM-5.5.6 expect its cyber risk oversight to work?
options: It is exempt from cyber governance rules
The CBB itself acts as its cyber risk function
Under a framework of policies ensuring adequate oversight by the regional or head office
Its local IT manager must chair the board's cyber committee
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.6 says branches of foreign banks must be governed under cyber risk policies that ensure an adequate level of oversight by the regional or head office.

quiz.question: The CISO notices that no one owns the bank's customer complaints database and it is missing from the inventory. Which OM-5.5.11 duties are not being met?
options: Clear ownership and classification of information assets, and a maintained inventory
The duty to buy cyber insurance
The duty to run a red team exercise
The duty to report to the CBB within one hour
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.11(a) and (b) require senior management to make sure all information assets and data have clear internal owners and classifications and are recorded in an inventory that is regularly reviewed.

quiz.question: According to OM-5.5.12, who should be involved when the bank classifies a set of data?
options: Only the external penetration testers
The customers whose data it is
Only the CBB's inspectors
The data owner, meaning the relevant business function
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.12 says the owner of the data, meaning the relevant business function, should be involved in classifying it, and that categories should be clear with little overlap.

quiz.question: In the CBB-hosted January 2024 copy of Module OM, how should a learner treat pages marked 'XX 2024', such as the external attack surface management paragraph?
options: As rules in force since July 2021
As guidance for Islamic banks only
As proposals from the consultation, to be confirmed against the final text
As withdrawn rules that no longer apply
quiz.explanation: The copy was published with the 28 January 2024 consultation; pages dated 'XX 2024' show proposed changes. Pages dated 2021 and 2022 show the rules then in force. Check the current Rulebook for the final position.

sessions.title: Prevention Controls, Phishing and Social Engineering
sessions.summary: Learn the preventive controls Module OM requires, the email and customer-link rules in OM-5.5.19 to OM-5.5.21, and how phishing, smishing, vishing, pretexting and payment-change fraud target bank staff and customers in Bahrain.
objectives: Describe the preventive controls listed in OM-5.5.18 and the anti-spoofing measures in OM-5.5.19
Apply OM-5.5.21's rules on email domains, SMS links and shortened links
Recognise phishing and social engineering red flags
Use the pause, verify and report routine

cards.title: The text message at the Riffa branch

lines.text: I'm Maryam Al Mahroos, contact centre supervisor. Three customers have called about a text saying their 'CPR details have expired' with a short link to fix it.
Short link, urgency, a request for ID details. That's a phishing pattern we've seen in Bahrain before.
One customer says the message looked like it came from us. Do we send links like that?
Not under our policy. Module OM limits links in SMS to messages the customer triggered, and bans shortened links in customer messages.
I'll check whether our email and SMS sender IDs are being spoofed, and whether any staff clicked.
And you, newcomer, will learn the controls that stop this, and the human habits that matter just as much.

scenes.heading: Endpoints
scenes.narration: Endpoint protection and endpoint detection and response tools, including anti-malware, find, block and isolate malicious code on laptops and servers.

scenes.heading: Network and web
scenes.narration: Firewalls segment the network, web application firewalls filter traffic to web apps, and network access control keeps unknown devices off physical ports.

scenes.heading: Email and browsing
scenes.narration: A secure email gateway filters malicious attachments, links and phishing, and a secure web gateway blocks harmful websites.

scenes.heading: Accounts
scenes.narration: Privileged access management and identity and access management limit and watch what powerful and ordinary accounts can do.

scenes.heading: Devices and data
scenes.narration: Mobile device management secures phones that reach bank systems, with encryption and remote wipe, and data leakage prevention stops confidential data leaving.

cards.title: Customer messages: what OM-5.5.21 allows
cards.caption: OM-5.5.21. Other domains may be used only with CBB approval in limited cases (OM-5.5.21A).

items.label: Email domain
items.left: One private bank domain or its subdomains

items.label: Links in SMS or WhatsApp
items.left: Only after a customer request or action
items.right: Unprompted links asking for data or payment

items.label: Extra safeguards
items.left: Clear instructions, a prior call, transaction details or authentication
items.right: A bare link with no context

items.label: Customer education
items.left: Campaigns explaining the bank's link rules

cards.question: Which measures does OM-5.5.19 give as examples of the anti-spoofing controls that prove the bank's emails are genuine?
options: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
VPN, MFA and PAM
SIEM, SOC and EDR
RTO, RPO and BCP
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.19 requires anti-spam and anti-spoofing measures that authenticate the bank's mail server, giving SPF, DKIM and DMARC as examples. The other sets are real controls but serve different purposes.

cards.title: Real case: the fake Benefitpay text (CBB warning, January 2021)
cards.body:
In **January 2021** the CBB published a warning about a fraudulent SMS. The message claimed the recipient's **Benefitpay account CPR number had expired** and told them to **update their CPR and activate the account** through a **shortened link**.

The CBB told the public **not to click the link** and said Benefitpay **never asks for personal information by SMS**.

What the attack used:

- a trusted local brand,
- a fake deadline and a threat of losing access,
- a request for identity details,
- a shortened link that hides the real destination.

This is why OM-5.5.21 bars shortened links in customer messages, limits SMS links to customer-initiated cases and asks banks to tell customers clearly what the bank will never send.

cards.title: Phishing red flag or normal?
cards.prompt: Sort each feature of a message received by a Dilmun Coast Bank employee.

items.text: Urgent warning that your account will be blocked today
A shortened link asking you to 'verify' your CPR details
Sender address on a free webmail domain using the bank's name
A request to keep a payment change secret from your manager
An internal system notice you can also find on the intranet
A calendar invite from a colleague for a meeting you agreed
A caller on a messaging app asking for a customer's one-time code
A payslip notice telling you to log in through the usual HR portal bookmark

cards.title: Social engineering: the attack on people
cards.body:
Technical controls stop many attacks, but criminals target staff because people can be persuaded. Common forms:

- **Phishing:** emails that copy a trusted brand to steal credentials or plant malware.
- **Smishing and vishing:** the same trick by SMS, messaging apps or phone, often with a fake caller ID.
- **Pretexting:** a believable story, such as 'I'm from head office audit', to get information.
- **Business email compromise:** a fake or hijacked executive or supplier email asking for an urgent payment or bank detail change.
- **Impersonating a regulator:** messages that copy an authority's logo and signature.

They all lean on **urgency, authority, fear or reward**. Your defence is a habit: **pause, verify through a channel you already trust, and report**. OM-5.5.22 also asks banks to consider **insider threats** in their threat assessments.

lines.text: One of my agents just got a call from someone saying he's from head office IT. He wanted her login code to 'fix the phishing problem'.
We never ask for codes or passwords. That's a vishing attempt riding on the SMS campaign.
She didn't give it. But she wasn't sure who to tell.
That gap matters. Every employee needs to know how to report straight to the SOC, quickly and without fear of blame.
Her report gives us the caller's number and the script. That helps us warn every branch within the hour.

cards.title: The supplier's new bank details
cards.situation: An email that appears to come from a long-standing IT supplier reaches Dilmun Coast Bank's accounts payable team. It says the supplier has changed banks and asks for this month's invoice of BHD 48,000 to be paid to a new account abroad. The sender address differs by one letter from the real one, and the message says the change is urgent and confidential.

choices.text: Pay the invoice to the new account, since the supplier is known and the invoice amount is correct.
choices.outcome: This is a classic business email compromise. The payment could be lost and is hard to recover once it leaves the bank.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking the supplier to confirm the change.
choices.outcome: Replying goes to the attacker, who will happily confirm. Verification must use a channel you already trust.

choices.text: Hold the payment, call the supplier on the number in the vendor master file, and report the email to the SOC.
choices.outcome: Right. Out-of-band verification stops the fraud, and the SOC can block the look-alike domain and warn other teams.

choices.text: Forward the email to colleagues to ask whether anyone else received it.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful for awareness, but forwarding spreads a malicious message and delays the report. Report it to the SOC instead.

cards.back: Endpoint detection and response: tools on devices that spot suspicious behaviour, alert and help contain it.
Data leakage prevention: detects and stops confidential data leaving the bank's technology environment.
Web application firewall: filters and monitors web traffic between a web application and the internet.
Privileged access management: secures, controls and monitors powerful administrator accounts.
A policy that tells receiving mail servers how to handle mail that fails sender checks, building on SPF and DKIM.
Only approved applications and components may run on the bank's systems.
A subscription service on emerging threats and criminal tools. Recommended in OM-5.5.20 and proposed as mandatory in 2024.

cards.title: Pause, verify, report
cards.caption: A simple staff routine that supports the bank's OM-5.5 controls and its regular cyber training.

items.label: Pause
items.detail: Urgency and secrecy are warning signs. Do not click, open or pay.

items.label: Check the sender
items.detail: Look at the real address, domain and number, not just the display name.

items.label: Verify independently
items.detail: Use a number or system you already trust, never the contact details in the message.

items.label: Report to the SOC
items.detail: Use the bank's phishing button or hotline, even if you clicked.

items.label: Help warn others
items.detail: The SOC blocks domains and alerts staff and, where needed, customers.

cards.question: A customer asks Maryam whether Dilmun Coast Bank ever sends payment links by SMS. Under OM-5.5.21, what is the right answer?
options: Yes, whenever the bank needs a payment
Only when the message results from the customer's own request or action, such as a payment they started
Never under any circumstances
Only through shortened links for security
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.21(a) limits links in SMS and short messages to those sent because of a customer request or action, such as onboarding verification or a customer-initiated payment. Shortened links are not allowed.

cards.title: If you clicked, say so fast
cards.body: Clicking a bad link is a mistake; hiding it is the real problem. Report at once, give the time and what you entered, and follow the SOC's instructions, such as disconnecting or changing your password. Early reports shorten the attacker's time inside the network and may help the bank meet its one-hour duty to contact the CBB when an incident qualifies.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: OM-5.5.18 requires layered preventive controls, including EDR, DLP, firewalls and WAF, secure email and web gateways, PAM, MDM, NAC and IAM.
OM-5.5.19 requires anti-spoofing email authentication such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
OM-5.5.21: one private email domain, SMS links only after customer action, no shortened links, extra safeguards and customer awareness campaigns.
Phishing, smishing, vishing, pretexting and payment-change fraud all exploit urgency, authority, fear or reward.
Staff routine: pause, verify through a trusted channel, report to the SOC quickly, even after a mistake.

cards.prompt: Think of the last unexpected message that asked you to act quickly. What would you check before acting, and how would you report it at your bank?

quiz.question: A marketing team at Dilmun Coast Bank wants to email customers from a popular free webmail address because the bank's domain has sending limits. What does OM-5.5.21 say?
options: Any domain is fine if the email carries the bank's logo
Free webmail is allowed for marketing but not for statements
Customer emails must use the bank's single private domain or its subdomains
The team only needs approval from the head of marketing
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.21 requires a single unified private email domain or its subdomains for customer communication and forbids third-party email provider domains. Other domains need CBB approval in limited cases under OM-5.5.21A.

quiz.question: Which item does OM-5.5.21 forbid in communications with customers?
options: Transaction amounts in alerts
The bank's own domain name
Instructions on how to use a link
Shortened links
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.21(b) tells banks to refrain from shortened links. Giving transaction details and clear instructions are among the safeguards the paragraph lists.

quiz.question: A customer starts an online card payment, and the bank sends a confirmation link by SMS showing the merchant name and amount. Is this consistent with OM-5.5.21?
options: No, links in SMS are banned in all cases
No, merchant names may not appear in SMS
Yes, the link follows a customer action and includes transaction details
Yes, but only if the link is shortened
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.21(a) allows links in short messages that result from customer requests or actions, such as payment links for customer-initiated transactions, and (c) lists giving the amount and merchant name as one safeguard.

quiz.question: What was the main lure in the fake Benefitpay SMS the CBB warned about in January 2021?
options: A prize draw for Benefitpay users
A claim that the user's CPR number had expired, with a link to update it
A request to call the CBB's hotline
An offer of a cheap personal loan
quiz.explanation: The CBB's warning showed an SMS claiming the Benefitpay account CPR number had expired and asking the user to update it through a shortened link. The CBB said Benefitpay never requests personal information by SMS.

quiz.question: Which OM-5.5.18 control is designed to stop confidential data leaving the bank's technology environment?
options: Data leakage prevention
A web application firewall
Network access control
Application whitelisting
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.18(b) requires data leakage prevention solutions to detect and prevent confidential data leaving. A WAF filters web traffic, NAC keeps unauthorised devices off the network and whitelisting limits which applications run.

quiz.question: An employee receives a call through a messaging app from someone claiming to be the bank's IT support, asking for her one-time login code to 'fix a problem'. What is the best response?
options: Refuse, end the call and report it to the SOC with the number and details
Give the code, since IT support needs it to help
Ask the caller to prove identity by giving her staff number
Give half the code and wait for a callback
quiz.explanation: Genuine IT staff never need your codes or passwords. Personal details can be found or guessed by attackers, so 'proof' from the caller is weak. Reporting helps the SOC warn others.

quiz.question: Under OM-5.5.20 in the January 2024 CBB copy of Module OM, what change is proposed for cyber threat intelligence services?
options: A subscription moves from recommended to mandatory
Subscriptions would be banned
Only the CBB would subscribe on behalf of banks
Subscriptions would be optional for retail banks
quiz.explanation: The 2024 copy shows 'should must' in OM-5.5.20, signalling that subscribing to a cyber threat intelligence service would become a requirement. Confirm the final text in the current Rulebook.

quiz.question: Which OM-5.5.21 duty is aimed at customers rather than at bank systems?
options: Configuring DMARC on the mail server
Awareness campaigns telling customers the bank will not send unprompted clickable links
Blocking shortened links in the SMS platform
Running weekly external vulnerability scans
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.21(d) requires customer awareness campaigns on link-related fraud, with clear instructions that the bank will not send clickable links asking for information or payment unless the customer started the action.

quiz.question: An email that seems to be from the chief executive asks a finance officer to make an urgent, confidential transfer to a new account and not to call because he is in a meeting. Which attack type is this most likely to be?
options: A denial of service attack
A web application attack
A ransomware encryption event
Business email compromise
quiz.explanation: A fake or hijacked executive or supplier email demanding an urgent, secret payment is the hallmark of business email compromise. The right step is to verify through a trusted channel and report it.

quiz.question: Which OM-5.5.18 control is meant to secure staff mobile phones that connect to bank systems, for example by enforcing encryption and allowing remote wipe?
options: A secure web gateway
Mobile device management with BYOD policies
Privileged access management
A web application firewall
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.18(i) requires mobile device management, including bring-your-own-device policies, to secure all mobile devices with access to bank systems through measures such as encryption, remote wipe and password enforcement.

sessions.title: Testing, Detection and Reporting Incidents to the CBB
sessions.summary: Cover cyber testing (threat and control assessments, vulnerability scans, penetration tests and red teaming), detection through the SIEM and SOC, the incident response roles and severity levels, and the CBB reporting duties in OM-5.5.57 to OM-5.5.61.
objectives: State the testing and reporting cycles for vulnerability scans, penetration tests and red teaming
Describe the SIEM, SOC, incident roles, incident log and severity levels
Apply the one-hour, two-hour and 10-calendar-day reporting steps for qualifying cyber incidents
Explain what the full incident report to the CBB must contain

cards.title: Alert at 02:10
cards.setting: Security Operations Centre, Seef. Wednesday, 2:10 am.

lines.text: SIEM alert: unusual data transfers from a customer database server to an unknown address. It started forty minutes ago.
Contain first. Isolate the server, keep the logs and open the incident log. Who's the incident owner tonight?
I am, under our playbook. I'll start the record and bring in the incident response team.
If customer information is compromised, the clock to the CBB has started. We have one hour to make contact.
Rashid here, I'm on the bridge. What do I need to decide, and by when?
Whether this is a critical incident for the crisis plan, and you'll approve what we tell the CBB. Arjun, show us what we know.

scenes.heading: Threat assessments
scenes.narration: Banks must assess cyber threats periodically: criminals, activists and insiders, attack methods, regional trends, dark web chatter and lessons from attacks on others.

scenes.heading: Control assessments
scenes.narration: Banks must also assess how mature and effective their controls are, and plan treatment for any risk above their tolerance.

scenes.heading: Vulnerability scans
scenes.narration: Regular technical scans cover internal systems, public-facing services and third-party connections, preferably monthly inside and weekly or more often outside.

scenes.heading: Patching
scenes.narration: Vulnerabilities found must be fixed and patches applied within a time that matches the risk each one poses.

scenes.heading: Penetration tests
scenes.narration: At least twice a year, certified testers simulate real attacks using recognised methods such as NIST or OWASP, with grey box and black box testing.

cards.title: Testing and log numbers in Module OM-5.5
cards.caption: From the CBB-hosted Module OM copy issued with the January 2024 consultation.

items.label: Penetration tests
items.detail: At least twice a year (OM-5.5.28).

items.label: Change test providers
items.detail: Internal and external independent testers changed at least every two years.

items.label: Pen test report to CBB
items.detail: Within two months after the end of the month of the test (OM-5.5.61).

items.label: Keep pen test reports
items.detail: From the date of the report, with mitigation steps.

items.label: Red team results
items.detail: To the CBB within one month of completion, with a fix plan, when required.

items.label: SIEM log retention
items.detail: Recommended in OM-5.5.33 to support investigations.

cards.question: Dilmun Coast Bank completes a penetration test in June. By when must the report reach the CBB under OM-5.5.61?
options: By 30 June
By 31 July
By 31 August
By 31 December
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.61 requires the report within two months after the end of the month of testing; the Rulebook's own example says a June test report is due by 31 August.

cards.title: Detecting and handling an incident
cards.body:
Module OM expects a bank to **see** incidents early and handle them in an orderly way:

- **SIEM:** a security information and event management system that collects data in real time from systems, applications and network devices and raises alerts (OM-5.5.31-5.5.32).
- **SOC:** a security operations centre that detects, investigates and responds to incidents and keeps the asset inventory and network diagrams (OM-5.5.35).
- **Scenarios:** risk scenarios and response plans tested and updated regularly, with new SIEM use cases for gaps (OM-5.5.36-5.5.37).
- **Escalation:** critical incidents go to the incident response team, management and the **board**, in line with the continuity and crisis plans (OM-5.5.38).
- **Containment:** isolate or shut down affected systems when needed, after weighing business impact (OM-5.5.34).
- **Records:** an incident log of every notification, decision and action, kept securely and in a legally admissible way (OM-5.5.41).

cards.title: Incident roles in OM-5.5.39
cards.prompt: Match each incident role or tool to what it does.

pairs.right: Leads detection and response for the incident and has authority to remove its impact
Manages consistent communication to internal and external stakeholders
Keeps an accurate record of the incident, actions and decisions for later review
Physical or virtual room where management gathers to handle a critical incident
Time-stamped record of notifications, decisions, actions, status and owner

cards.title: Severity levels suggested in OM-5.5.42
cards.caption: A pre-set severity framework helps teams classify quickly and consistently.

items.label: Severity 1
items.left: Serious disruption or degradation of critical services
items.right: Potentially high impact on public confidence

items.label: Severity 3
items.left: Little or no impact on critical services
items.right: No visible impact on public confidence

lines.text: Confirmed: the attacker copied part of a customer table with names and phone numbers. The server is isolated.
Customer information is compromised. Under OM-5.5.57 we must contact the CBB immediately, within one hour, by phone.
We don't know the root cause yet. Shouldn't we wait until we have the full picture?
No. The call comes first, then Section A of the incident report by email within two hours. The full Section B follows within 10 calendar days.
And weekly progress updates to the CBB until it's fully resolved. I'll make sure the record keeper logs every step.

cards.title: Reporting a qualifying cyber incident to the CBB
cards.prompt: Put Dilmun Coast Bank's reporting steps in order, following OM-5.5.57 to OM-5.5.58.
steps: Detect the incident and confirm it compromises customer information or disrupts critical services
Contact the CBB by telephone immediately, within one hour
Email Section A of the Cyber Security Incident Report to the CBB's incident address within two hours
Submit Section B with root cause, impact and measures within 10 calendar days of the incident
Send weekly progress updates to the CBB until the incident is fully resolved

cards.title: Report now or later?
cards.situation: At 3:00 am a ransomware attack takes Dilmun Coast Bank's card authorisation system offline for retail customers. The team is confident it can restore from backup by 9:00 am. The head of IT suggests telling the CBB only after restoration, 'so we report good news, not panic'.

choices.text: Agree: report once services are back, with a complete story.
choices.outcome: This breaks OM-5.5.57. A disruption of critical services that affects operations requires contact with the CBB within one hour, whatever the expected recovery time.

choices.text: Call the CBB within one hour, send Section A within two hours, then Section B within 10 calendar days and weekly updates.
choices.outcome: Right. The rule is triggered by disruption of critical services, and early contact lets the CBB judge any wider impact. Restoration updates go in the follow-up reports.

choices.text: Email the CBB a short note after 24 hours, as an overnight incident is not 'immediate'.
choices.outcome: The time limit runs from occurrence or detection, day or night. A delayed email misses both the one-hour call and the two-hour Section A deadline.

choices.text: Call the CBB within one hour but skip Section A, since the full report will follow.
choices.outcome: The call is right, but Section A is still due within two hours. Partial compliance leaves the bank in breach.

cards.back: A penetration test where testers have partial knowledge of the system, such as a user account or design notes.
A penetration test where testers start with no inside knowledge, like an outside attacker.
A targeted exercise, which the CBB may require, testing the bank's detection and response across cyber, social and physical fronts.
A quiet attack spread over a long time to avoid detection, which is why long log retention helps.
Malware information sharing platforms, where banks may share non-sensitive threat data such as indicators of compromise.
How long an attacker has undetected access until fully removed: a key incident performance metric.

cards.title: Real case: the CBB's readiness statement (March 2026)

cards.question: Which incidents trigger the OM-5.5.57 duty to contact the CBB within one hour?
options: Only incidents that cause financial loss above a set threshold
Any internal or external cyber incident that compromises customer information or disrupts critical services affecting operations
Only attacks confirmed by the police
Only incidents rated Severity 1 that last more than a day
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.57 covers any cyber security incident, internal or external, that compromises customer information or disrupts critical services that affect operations. It sets no money threshold or minimum duration.

cards.title: Report with what you have
cards.body: OM-5.5.59 says the bank should send its report with as much information as possible even if not all details are known yet. Do not hold a report back to perfect it. Log the time of every call and email so the bank can show it met the one-hour and two-hour limits.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Periodic threat and control assessments, vulnerability scans (preferably monthly internal, weekly external) and risk-based patching are required.
Penetration tests at least twice a year by certified testers, providers changed at least every two years, reports to the CBB within two months after the test month.
A SIEM and SOC detect incidents; critical incidents are escalated to the response team, management and the board.
Named roles (incident owner, spokesperson, record keeper), a situation room and an incident log support an orderly response.
Qualifying incidents: call the CBB within one hour, Section A within two hours, Section B within 10 calendar days, then weekly updates.

cards.prompt: If you discovered a suspected incident at 2 am, who would you call first at your bank, and do you know where the incident reporting playbook is kept?

quiz.question: How often must Dilmun Coast Bank carry out penetration testing of its systems, applications and network devices under OM-5.5.28?
options: At least twice a year
Once every three years
Only after a major incident
Once a quarter, by the internal team only
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.28 requires penetration testing at least twice a year, using internal and external independent testers who are changed at least every two years.

quiz.question: Which description fits the vulnerability assessment frequency OM-5.5.25 prefers?
options: Yearly for all systems
Daily for internal systems and monthly for public-facing ones
Only before new systems go live
Monthly for internal technology, and weekly or more often for public-facing services
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.25 says assessments are preferably monthly for internal technology and weekly or more frequent for external, public-facing services and systems.

quiz.question: The CBB asks Dilmun Coast Bank to run a red teaming exercise. What must the bank do with the results under OM-5.5.30?
options: Keep them internally and show them at the next inspection
Publish them in the annual report
Send them to the CBB within 10 calendar days without a plan
Give them to the CBB within one month of completion, with a plan to fix weaknesses
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.30 requires red team results to reach the CBB within one month of completing the exercise, together with a comprehensive plan to address observed weaknesses.

quiz.question: What does OM-5.5.33 recommend for keeping SIEM logs?
options: Delete them after 30 days to protect privacy
Retain them for five years or longer to support investigations
Keep them for one year only
Keep only logs from incidents reported to the CBB
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.33 says banks should keep SIEM logs and related information for five years or longer, including to investigate 'low-and-slow' attacks.

quiz.question: In the incident response roles described in OM-5.5.39, who manages consistent communication to internal and external stakeholders?
options: The Record Keeper
The Incident Owner
The Spokesperson
The external penetration tester
quiz.explanation: The Spokesperson, from external communications or another suitable department, consolidates information and keeps stakeholders updated consistently. The Record Keeper documents the incident; the Incident Owner leads the response.

quiz.question: At 10:00 the SOC confirms an intrusion has exposed customer account details. By when must Dilmun Coast Bank, a retail bank, have sent Section A of the Cyber Security Incident Report?
options: By 12:00, within two hours
By 11:00, within one hour
By the end of the next business day
Within 10 calendar days
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.57 requires contacting the CBB immediately, within one hour, by phone, and sending Section A to the CBB's incident email within two hours. Section B is due within 10 calendar days.

quiz.question: What must Section B of the Cyber Security Incident Report contain under OM-5.5.58?
options: Full root cause analysis, business and customer impact, and the measures taken
Only the time the incident was detected
The names of staff to be disciplined
A press release for the media
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.58 requires all relevant details, including full root cause analysis, impact on operations and customers, and all measures taken to stop the attack, limit impact and prevent recurrence.

quiz.question: After Section B is submitted, the bank is still cleaning up the incident. What does OM-5.5.58 require?
options: Nothing more until the next annual report
Weekly progress updates to the CBB until it is fully resolved
A monthly update to the board only
A new Section A every day
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.58 requires a weekly progress update to the CBB until the incident is fully resolved.

quiz.question: Under OM-5.5.42, which description matches a Severity 2 incident?
options: Serious disruption of critical services and high impact on public confidence
Some degradation of critical services and a medium impact on public confidence
No impact on critical services or public confidence
Any incident caused by a third-party provider
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.42 describes Severity 1 as serious disruption with high confidence impact, Severity 2 as some degradation with medium impact and Severity 3 as little or no impact.

quiz.question: Which set of features must penetration tests include under OM-5.5.28?
options: Only automated scanning tools run by IT staff
Testing only on old copies of systems, never production
A recognised method, grey and black box testing, and certified testers
A single external firm used permanently
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.28 requires a risk-based approach on a recognised method such as NIST or OWASP, grey box and black box testing, certified professionals, rotated internal and external testers, and testing on production or exact replicas.

sessions.title: Customer Confidentiality and Personal Data: CBB Law and PDPL
sessions.summary: Apply the confidentiality rules in Articles 116 to 119 of the CBB Law, recognise attempts to obtain customer information by deception, link data classification and leakage controls to confidentiality, and place the Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018) in general terms.
objectives: Define confidential information and the four disclosure gateways under Articles 116-117 of the CBB Law
Explain how Articles 118, 119 and 171 extend and enforce confidentiality
Handle third-party requests for customer information safely
Describe the PDPL and its supervisor in general terms

cards.title: The caller who knew too much

lines.text: A caller says he's a lawyer for a customer's family. He wants the customer's balance and recent transfers 'for an urgent family matter'.
Does the customer know? Is there a court order or a CBB instruction?
No. He says the customer is in hospital and can't speak. He sounds genuine and upset.
Then we can't disclose. The CBB Law treats information on a customer's private affairs as confidential, with only a few legal gateways.
And it fits the pattern from the data theft last week. Callers use stolen names and phone numbers to sound convincing.
This stage is about keeping secrets: the CBB Law, data protection in Bahrain and the tricks people use to get information out of us.

scenes.heading: What is confidential
scenes.narration: Article 116 of the CBB Law defines confidential information as any information on the private affairs of a licensee's customers.

scenes.heading: Four gateways
scenes.narration: Article 117 says a licensee may disclose it only with the customer's unequivocal approval, under a law or international agreement, to carry out a court order, or to follow a CBB instruction.

scenes.heading: The CBB's own powers
scenes.narration: Article 118 lets the CBB disclose information it receives in those cases, to protect the stability and trust of the financial system, and when cooperating with international or competent bodies.

scenes.heading: It follows the data
scenes.narration: Article 119 says anyone who receives confidential information may only disclose it as Article 118 allows.

scenes.heading: Serious consequences
scenes.narration: In the CBB-hosted English text, Article 171 provides imprisonment and a fine of up to 10,000 Bahraini dinars, or either, for disclosing confidential information in bad faith.

cards.title: Can Dilmun Coast Bank disclose this customer information?
cards.caption: Articles 116-117 of the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law (Law No. 64 of 2006).

items.label: Is it about a customer's private affairs?
items.detail: If yes, Article 116 makes it confidential information.

items.label: Clear customer approval?
items.detail: Unequivocal approval from the person the information relates to.

items.label: Required by law or treaty?
items.detail: A provision of law or an international agreement Bahrain has signed.

items.label: Court order?
items.detail: Executing an order of a competent court.

items.label: CBB instruction?
items.detail: Implementing an instruction given by the Central Bank.

items.label: None applies: do not disclose
items.detail: Escalate to compliance or legal if in doubt.

cards.title: Disclosure allowed or not?
cards.prompt: Under Article 117, sort each request to Dilmun Coast Bank.

items.text: The customer signs a clear consent letting her accountant see her statements
A competent court orders the bank to produce account records
The CBB instructs the bank to provide information on an account
A caller claiming to be the customer's lawyer asks for balances by phone
A relative of a customer in hospital asks for recent transfers
A journalist asks whether a well-known businessman banks with you
A disclosure required by a law of Bahrain
A colleague in marketing asks for a list of high-balance customers for a personal side business

cards.question: Under Article 117 of the CBB Law, which situation lets Dilmun Coast Bank disclose a customer's account details?
options: A close relative asks in person and shows ID
The bank receives an order issued by a competent court
A senior manager approves the request internally
The requester promises to keep the details private
cards.explanation: Article 117 allows disclosure with the customer's unequivocal approval, under law or an international agreement, to execute a competent court's order, or to implement a CBB instruction. A relative's request or internal approval are not gateways.

cards.title: Personal data protection in general terms
The spreadsheet on the shared drive

lines.text: Internal audit found a spreadsheet of 3,000 customers with CPR numbers and salaries on a shared drive anyone can open.
That breaks our data classification. Under OM-5.5.12 the owner decides who can access data, how it's secured, kept and disposed of.
My team used it last year for a campaign. I didn't think about who else could see it.
Lock it down now, find out who opened it and check the DLP alerts. If it left the bank, we treat it as a possible incident.
And we fix the root cause: training and a clear rule on where customer lists may be stored.

cards.title: A request from 'head office'
cards.situation: Maryam receives an email from an address that looks like the bank's regional office. It asks her to send a list of the Riffa branch's top 50 customers with phone numbers 'for a CBB data request due today'. The email carries the bank's logo and a senior manager's signature block.

choices.text: Send the list quickly, as the CBB deadline is today and the sender looks senior.
choices.outcome: Urgency, authority and a copied signature are classic social engineering signs. Sending the list could breach the CBB Law's confidentiality rules and the bank's data policies.

choices.text: Check the request through a known channel, such as calling compliance on the internal directory number, and report the email to the SOC.
choices.outcome: Right. A genuine CBB request comes through compliance with a record of the instruction. Verifying independently protects customers and catches the attack.

choices.text: Send only names without phone numbers to reduce the risk.
choices.outcome: Customer names linked to the bank are still information on their private affairs. Partial disclosure to an unverified sender is still a breach.

choices.text: Reply asking the sender to confirm it is genuine.
choices.outcome: Better than sending, but a reply goes straight back to the attacker. Use a channel you already trust.

cards.title: Real case: impersonating a regulator (CBB warning, June 2019)

cards.front: Myth: family members can get details if the customer is ill.
cards.back: Fact: without unequivocal customer approval or another Article 117 gateway, the bank must not disclose.

cards.front: Myth: confirming that someone is a customer is harmless.
cards.back: Fact: even the existence of a relationship can be information on a customer's private affairs.

cards.front: Myth: once information leaves the bank, the duty ends.
cards.back: Fact: Article 119 limits further disclosure by anyone who receives confidential information.

cards.front: Myth: internal colleagues can see any customer data.
cards.back: Fact: access follows data classification and need to know (OM-5.5.12).

cards.front: Myth: data protection replaces banking secrecy.
cards.back: Fact: the PDPL adds general data duties; the CBB Law's confidentiality rules still apply to banks.

cards.title: Protecting customer data day to day
cards.caption: Combines the CBB Law's confidentiality rules with the data classification and DLP controls in Module OM.

items.label: Classify
items.detail: Know which data is confidential and who owns it.

items.label: Limit access
items.detail: Only those who need it, through approved systems.

items.label: Verify requests
items.detail: Check identity and the legal gateway before any disclosure.

items.label: Store and share safely
items.detail: Approved locations, encryption where required, no personal email.

items.label: Report and review
items.detail: Report leaks or odd requests at once; learn from them.

cards.question: Which statement about Bahrain's Personal Data Protection Law is accurate at the level this quest teaches?
options: It is Law No. 30 of 2018 and is supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority
It replaced the confidentiality articles of the CBB Law
It applies only to government bodies
It is a CBB Rulebook module
cards.explanation: The PDPL is Law No. 30 of 2018, supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority. It applies alongside, not instead of, the CBB Law's confidentiality rules, and it is a law, not a Rulebook module.

cards.title: Phone requests: a simple script
cards.body: When a caller asks about a customer's affairs: 1) do not confirm or deny the relationship; 2) explain politely that the bank can only discuss accounts with the customer or under legal authority; 3) offer to take a message and call the customer on the number already held; 4) log and report suspicious calls to the SOC. Never let sympathy or pressure override the rule.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Article 116 of the CBB Law: confidential information is any information on a customer's private affairs.
Article 117 gateways: unequivocal customer approval, law or international agreement, competent court order, or CBB instruction.
Article 119 extends the limit to anyone who receives confidential information; bad-faith disclosure is an offence (Article 171).
The PDPL (Law No. 30 of 2018), supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority, adds general data protection duties.
Social engineers use urgency, authority, sympathy and copied logos: verify through trusted channels and report.

cards.prompt: Recall a time someone asked you for information about another person. How did you check they were entitled to it, and what would you do differently now?

quiz.question: How does Article 116 of the CBB Law define confidential information?
options: Only account balances above a set amount
Only information marked 'confidential' by the bank
Any information on the private affairs of a licensee's customers
Only information about corporate customers
quiz.explanation: Article 116 defines confidential information broadly as any information on the private affairs of any of the licensee's customers. It is not limited by amount, labelling or customer type.

quiz.question: A customer emails Dilmun Coast Bank: 'Please send my last three statements to my accountant at this address.' She signs it and the bank verifies the request with her. Which Article 117 gateway applies?
options: A competent court order
A CBB instruction
The customer's unequivocal approval
No gateway, so the bank must refuse
quiz.explanation: Article 117 allows disclosure with the unequivocal approval of the person the information relates to. A clear, verified instruction from the customer meets that test.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four disclosure gateways in Article 117 of the CBB Law?
options: Executing an order of a competent court
Approval by the bank's chief executive
Implementing a CBB instruction
Compliance with a law or an international agreement signed by Bahrain
quiz.explanation: The four gateways are customer approval, law or international agreement, a competent court order and a CBB instruction. Internal approval by bank management is not a gateway.

quiz.question: A company receives confidential customer information from a bank under a valid gateway. Under Article 119, may it pass the information on freely?
options: No, it may only disclose it as Article 118 permits
Yes, once it has left the bank the duty ends
Yes, if it pays a fee to the CBB
Only to its own shareholders
quiz.explanation: Article 119 says no person who receives confidential information directly or indirectly may disclose it except as Article 118 allows. The duty follows the information.

quiz.question: In the CBB-hosted English text of the CBB Law, what does Article 171 provide for a person who discloses confidential information in bad faith?
options: Imprisonment and a fine of up to BD 10,000, or either penalty
A written warning only
A fine of up to BD 500
Loss of the bank's licence automatically
quiz.explanation: Article 171 provides imprisonment and a fine not exceeding 10,000 Bahraini dinars, or either penalty, without prejudice to greater penalties in other laws.

quiz.question: Which authority supervises Bahrain's Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018)?
options: The National Cybersecurity Center
The Personal Data Protection Authority
The CBB's Consumer Protection Office
The Ministry of Interior's financial intelligence unit
quiz.explanation: The PDPL is supervised by the Personal Data Protection Authority. The NCSC is the national cyber security body, and the CBB supervises banks under the CBB Law.

quiz.question: A caller says he is a customer's brother, gives the customer's full name, CPR number and phone number correctly, and asks for the account balance. What should Maryam's agent do?
options: Decline, offer to contact the customer on the number on file, and log the call
Give the balance, since he passed the identity checks
Give the balance but not the transactions
Ask for the customer's date of birth and then disclose
quiz.explanation: Knowing a customer's details does not make someone the customer or create an Article 117 gateway. Stolen data is often used this way, so the agent should refuse, contact the customer through known details and log the call.

quiz.question: Under OM-5.5.12, which question should a bank's data classification policy answer?
options: Which marketing campaign the data will be used for next
Who has access to the data and how long it is retained
How much the data could sell for
Which customers have the highest balances
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.12 lists access, security, retention including backups, disposal method, encryption and appropriate use as aspects the classification policy should decide.

quiz.question: What did the CBB's June 2019 warning say criminals were doing when they impersonated CySEC?
options: Hacking the CBB's website
Opening branches without a licence
Selling counterfeit banknotes
Sending genuine-looking emails with copied logos and signatures and seeking fees and personal data
quiz.explanation: The CBB described emails carrying CySEC's name, stamp, logo and copied signatures, false compensation promises, requests for personal information and follow-up calls.

quiz.question: How does the PDPL relate to the confidentiality rules in the CBB Law for a Bahraini bank?
options: The PDPL cancels the CBB Law's confidentiality articles
Only the PDPL applies to banks
Only the CBB Law applies, as banks are exempt from the PDPL
Both apply: the PDPL adds general data duties alongside banking confidentiality
quiz.explanation: Banks must respect the CBB Law's confidentiality rules and the general data protection duties of the PDPL. Check specific PDPL duties with your bank's data protection lead.

sessions.title: Training, Awareness, Recovery and Readiness for the CBB
sessions.summary: Bring it together: the training duties in OM-5.5.54 to OM-5.5.56 for all employees, higher-risk staff, the board and senior management, measuring effectiveness, exercises, recovery, cyber insurance and the evidence a bank needs for a CBB review.
objectives: Explain the cyber training duties for all employees, higher-risk staff, the executive board, senior management, cyber and IT staff
Show how to evaluate whether training improves awareness and preparedness
Describe recovery objectives, exercises, continuity planning and cyber insurance under Module OM
Assemble the evidence the bank needs to show the CBB its cyber programme works

cards.title: The training numbers that didn't add up

lines.text: Our cyber training completion rate is 98%. That sounds excellent. Why does Fatema look unhappy?
Because completion isn't the test. OM-5.5.54 asks us to evaluate whether awareness and preparedness actually improve.
Our last phishing simulation: 21% of staff clicked, and only 6% reported it. The year before it was about the same.
So the board report says 'trained', but behaviour hasn't changed. That's what the CBB will look at.
My agents get the same generic video as the IT team. They face phone scams all day, but nothing covers those.
Then our final stage is clear: build training that fits each role, measure it honestly and get ready to show the CBB.

scenes.heading: Everyone, regularly
scenes.narration: All employees must receive adequate cyber security training on a regular basis about the threats they could meet.

scenes.heading: Practice, not just theory
scenes.narration: Training can include testing how employees react to simulated cyber attacks, such as mock phishing emails.

scenes.heading: Current threats
scenes.narration: All relevant employees must be kept informed of current cyber security breaches and threats.

scenes.heading: More for higher-risk staff
scenes.narration: Higher-risk staff should get additional training, and role-specific training must be given regularly to the executive board and senior management, cyber roles, IT staff and other high-risk staff.

scenes.heading: Prove it works
scenes.narration: The bank must evaluate improvement in awareness and preparedness, so it knows its training programmes are effective.

cards.title: Role-specific cyber training at Dilmun Coast Bank
cards.caption: From the CBB-hosted Module OM copy issued with the January 2024 consultation; the training paragraphs sit on pages dated July 2021 and April 2022.

items.label: Executive board and senior management
items.detail: Role-specific training on cyber risk oversight, reports and crisis decisions (OM-5.5.56(a)).

items.label: Cyber security roles
items.detail: Regular updates and certification-level courses, such as CISSP or CISM (OM-5.5.11(d) and OM-5.5.56(b)).

items.label: IT staff
items.detail: Role-specific training on secure configuration, change and access (OM-5.5.56(c)).

items.label: High-risk staff
items.detail: Extra training for roles the bank identifies, such as payments or contact centre (OM-5.5.55-56).

items.label: All employees
items.detail: Regular awareness training, simulations and threat updates (OM-5.5.55).

cards.title: Who needs what training?
cards.prompt: Match each group with the training Module OM expects.

pairs.right: Adequate, regular cyber training, including reactions to simulated attacks
Additional training beyond the general programme
Regular update and training sessions to keep up with threats and countermeasures
Reports at every meeting that include staff awareness status

cards.question: Dilmun Coast Bank's training completion rate is 98%, but phishing simulation results have not improved in two years. Which OM-5.5 requirement is most at risk?
options: OM-5.5.54: evaluating improvement in awareness to make sure training is effective
OM-5.5.53: cyber insurance
OM-5.5.21: single email domain
OM-5.5.28: penetration testing
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.54 requires the bank to evaluate improvement in awareness and preparedness to make sure training programmes are effective. Completion alone does not show that.

cards.title: Recovery, exercises and insurance
cards.body:
Training is wider than courses. Module OM also expects banks to **practise** and **prepare to recover**:

- **Recovery objectives:** identify critical systems and set **recovery time objectives (RTO)** and **recovery point objectives (RPO)**; critical systems must be able to recover within the defined RTO (OM-5.5.45-5.5.48).
- **Clean restoration:** check that recovered systems are free of compromise and data is intact before returning to normal (OM-5.5.49).
- **Exercises:** a programme of attack simulations, **war games** and **table-top** exercises involving technical staff, the crisis team, decision-makers and spokespersons (OM-5.5.50).
- **Communication:** accurate, timely updates to internal stakeholders, including the board (OM-5.5.51).
- **Continuity:** the business continuity plan must include recovery from cyber incidents (OM-5.5.52).
- **Insurance:** seek cyber risk insurance after a risk assessment independently verified by the insurer (OM-5.5.53).

cards.title: Effective training or tick-box?
cards.prompt: Sort each element of a cyber training programme.

items.text: Phishing simulation click and report rates tracked over time
A single annual video for every role
Contact centre scenarios on vishing and pretext calls
Counting attendance without testing understanding
Table-top exercise for the executive team on the CBB one-hour call
Monthly bulletins on current threats seen by the SOC
Training slides unchanged for three years

lines.text: Scenario: it's 6 am on a weekend. Online banking is down after a ransomware attack, and customers are posting on social media.
First decision: is this a critical incident under our crisis plan? I think yes.
Then the clock to the CBB has started. Who makes the call, and who has the number?
And what do my agents tell customers who call? We need a script within the hour.
Good. These gaps are exactly what OM-5.5.50 exercises are for. We'll fix them before a real attack finds them.

cards.title: Designing next year's programme
cards.situation: Fatema asks you to propose next year's cyber training plan for the executive committee. The budget allows one major change.

choices.text: Buy a longer generic e-learning course for everyone and require 100% completion.
choices.outcome: More content does not show effectiveness, and it ignores role-specific needs for executives, IT, cyber and high-risk staff.

choices.text: Build a role-based programme with regular simulations, threat bulletins, extra modules for high-risk staff and executive table-tops, and measure results over time.
choices.outcome: Right. This covers OM-5.5.55 and OM-5.5.56 and gives the evidence OM-5.5.54 asks for, which can also feed the board's awareness report.

choices.text: Train only the IT and cyber teams, since they handle the systems.
choices.outcome: OM-5.5.55 requires training for all employees, and phishing targets everyone. Specialist training is needed but is not enough.

choices.text: Keep the current course but add one phishing simulation a year.
choices.outcome: A step forward, but a single yearly test gives little evidence of improvement and misses role-specific training.

cards.title: Readiness checklist for a CBB review

cards.back: Board-approved policy (reviewed at least annually), framework evaluated within three years, cyber on board agendas, minutes and reports.
Qualified CISO, independent cyber risk function, adequate cyber staff with current training.
Twice-yearly penetration tests, reports sent to the CBB on time and kept for five years, scan results and patch records.
Playbooks, incident logs, named roles and evidence of one-hour and two-hour reporting to the CBB.
Role-based plan, simulation results, threat bulletins and evidence of improvement.
Single email domain, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, link rules and customer awareness campaigns.

items.label: Call the CBB
items.detail: After a qualifying cyber incident (OM-5.5.57).

items.label: Section A by email
items.detail: Initial Cyber Security Incident Report (OM-5.5.57).

items.label: Section B
items.detail: Full report within 10 calendar days, then weekly updates (OM-5.5.58).

items.label: Pen test report
items.detail: After the end of the test month (OM-5.5.61).

items.label: Cyber policy review
items.detail: At least annually (OM-5.5.15).

items.label: Framework and strategy
items.detail: Framework evaluated and strategy revised at least every three years (OM-5.5.5, 5.5.14).

cards.title: Real case: CBB and NCSC awareness event (August 2026)

cards.question: Which groups must receive regular role-specific cyber security training under OM-5.5.56?
options: Only the IT department
Executive board and senior management, cyber security roles, IT staff and high-risk staff the bank identifies
Only new joiners in their first month
Only customers using digital channels
cards.explanation: OM-5.5.56 lists the executive board and senior management, cyber security roles, IT staff and any high-risk staff as determined by the licensee. OM-5.5.55 separately covers all employees.

cards.title: Make your board report count
cards.body: Report training as outcomes, not just attendance: simulation click and report rates by department, time to report, repeat clickers given extra coaching, and lessons from real incidents. OM-5.5.4 expects staff awareness status in the board's cyber reports, so give directors numbers they can challenge.

cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: OM-5.5.55: all employees get adequate, regular cyber training, can be tested with simulated attacks and are kept informed of current threats.
OM-5.5.56: regular role-specific training for the executive board and senior management, cyber roles, IT staff and high-risk staff.
OM-5.5.54: the bank must evaluate whether awareness and preparedness improve, so training is shown to be effective.
Exercises (simulations, war games, table-tops), RTO and RPO, clean recovery, cyber in the BCP and cyber insurance complete the picture.
Be ready to show the CBB evidence: policies, reports, test results, incident logs, reporting times and training outcomes.

cards.prompt: Which cyber threat is most likely to target your own role, and what one training or practice change would make you better prepared for it?

quiz.question: Which group does OM-5.5.55 say must receive adequate cyber security training on a regular basis?
options: Only IT staff
Only staff who handle payments
All employees
Only board members
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.55 requires that all employees receive adequate, regular training on cyber security and the threats they could encounter. Role-specific training under OM-5.5.56 comes on top.

quiz.question: Which method does OM-5.5.55 give as an example of how cyber training can be delivered?
options: Asking staff to sign the policy each year
Testing employee reactions to simulated cyber attack scenarios
Sending the policy to staff by post
Holding a quiz only for new joiners
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.55 mentions testing employee reactions to simulated cyber attack scenarios, such as mock phishing, as one way to deliver the training.

quiz.question: Dilmun Coast Bank decides its payments operations team is high-risk. What does Module OM expect for that team?
options: Additional and role-specific training on top of the general programme
An exemption from the general programme
Training only after an incident
Penetration testing of each team member
quiz.explanation: OM-5.5.55 says higher-risk staff should get additional training, and OM-5.5.56(d) requires role-specific training for any high-risk staff the bank identifies.

quiz.question: What does OM-5.5.54 require the bank to do about its cyber training programmes?
options: Have them approved by the CBB before each session
